extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; policymakers; educated public
extracted.subtask_description: Identification and explanation of the causes that promote or impede the prosperity, population, and improvement of new colonies, with historical examples from European empires. The excerpt gives evaluative principles (economic, legal, institutional, and cultural) for why some colonies prospered more than others.

rubrics_metrics.name: The sacred thirst of gold
rubrics_metrics.description: All the other enterprises of the Spaniards in the New World...seem to have been prompted by the same motive. It was the sacred thirst of gold that carried Ovieda, Nicuessa, and Vasco Nugnes de Balboa, to the Isthmus of Darien; that carried Cortes to Mexico, Almagro and Pizarro to Chili and Peru.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an explanatory criterion for motives of conquest and settlement: explorers and settlers first inquire whether gold exists and decide to settle or leave based on that. Examples: Columbus, Cortes, Pizarro, Sir Walter Raleigh and the El Dorado myth; warns that avarice, not pious motives, primarily drove many colonial enterprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation reduces mining incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Columbus proposed that half of all the gold and silver found should belong to the crown...The rigorous exaction of it...first occasioned the total abandoning of the mines of St. Domingo...It was soon reduced, therefore, to a third; then to a fifth; afterwards to a tenth; and at last to a twentieth part of the gross produce of the gold mines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical evidence that heavy crown/tax claims can destroy the profitability of mine workings and lead to abandonment; shows how tax rates and fiscal policy affect resource exploitation and colonial economic activity. Mentions silver tax remained a fifth long and only reduced later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for new mines is ruinous
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all those expensive and uncertain projects...there is none, perhaps, more perfectly ruinous than the search after new silver and gold mines. It is, perhaps, the most disadvantageous lottery in the world...Projects of mining, instead of replacing the capital employed in them...commonly absorb both capital and profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames mining ventures as high-risk, low-expected-return investments that often bankrupt participants; warns lawmakers and investors against extraordinary encouragement of mining projects because they divert capital unproductively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of metals arises from scarcity and extraction costs
rubrics_metrics.description: They did not consider that the value of those metals has, in all ages and nations, arisen chiefly from their scarcity, and that their scarcity has arisen from the very small quantities of them which nature has anywhere deposited in one place, from the hard and intractable substances with which she has almost everywhere surrounded those small quantities, and consequently from the labour and expense which are everywhere necessary in order to penetrate, and get at them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why expectations of abundant precious-metal veins are delusional; cautions against equating the apparent finds of early adventurers with sustainable wealth. Uses El Dorado as an example of persistent, even learned, delusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonies carry superior knowledge and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The colonies carry out with them a knowledge of agriculture and of other useful arts, superior to what can grow up of its own accord...They carry out with them, too, the habit of subordination, some notion of the regular government...and of a regular administration of justice; and they naturally establish something of the same kind in the new settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies transfer of skills, institutions, and legal/governmental practices from mother country as a central cause of faster material and cultural improvement in colonies versus indigenous societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plenty of good land and low rents encourage improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Every colonist gets more land than he can possibly cultivate. He has no rent, and scarce any taxes, to pay. No landlord shares with him in its produce...He has every motive to render as great as possible a produce which is thus to be almost entirely his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that abundant, cheap, or free land gives strong private incentives to improve and cultivate land, which in turn drives population growth, higher wages, and overall prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: High wages incentivize population and settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Those liberal wages, joined to the plenty and cheapness of land, soon make those labourers leave him, in order to become landlords themselves...The liberal reward of labour encourages marriage...When arrived at maturity, the high price of labour, and the low price of land, enable them to establish themselves in the same manner as their fathers did before them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connects labor scarcity and high wages to demographic expansion and social mobility: high wages attract labour, encourage family formation, and enable labourers to become landholders, strengthening colony growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engrossing of uncultivated land obstructs improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The engrossing of uncultivated land...is the greatest obstruction to its improvement...The colony law, which imposes upon every proprietor the obligation of improving and cultivating, within a limited time, a certain proportion of his lands...has, however, had some effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques land monopolization (engrossing) as harming the availability of cheap land and thus blocking the incentives to cultivate and employ labour; endorses legal mechanisms that require improvement and allow regranting of neglected land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance rules shape land division and economic dynamism
rubrics_metrics.description: In Pennsylvania there is no right of primogeniture, and lands...are divided equally among all the children...In the other English colonies, indeed, the right of primogeniture takes place...In the Spanish and Portuguese colonies, what is called the right of majorazzo takes place...Such estates go all to one person, and are in effect entailed and unalienable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how succession laws (primogeniture, equal division, majorazzo, custom of Paris) affect alienation, subdivision, and circulation of land: more equal or alienable tenures encourage quicker division by sale and thus broader access to land, aiding prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate civil taxes let colonists accumulate capital
rubrics_metrics.description: The labour of the English colonists is...likely to afford a greater and more valuable produce, but, in consequence of the moderation of their taxes, a greater proportion of this produce belongs to themselves, which they may store up and employ in putting into motion a still greater quantity of labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that lower civil taxation increases savings and investment in the colony, facilitating capital accumulation and economic development. Provides concrete civil expenditure figures for English colonies as evidence of low civil cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive companies hinder colonial commerce and growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Some nations have given up the whole commerce of their colonies to an exclusive company...It was the interest of the company...to sell the former as dear, and to buy the latter as cheap as possible...Of all the expedients that can well be contrived to stunt the natural growth of a new colony, that of an exclusive company is undoubtedly the most effectual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies monopoly trading companies as a major policy error: they depress colonial producers' returns, discourage growth of surplus produce, and stunt natural population and economic expansion. Examples: Dutch and Danish companies' effects; improvements after dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relaxed monopoly / free trade or licenses improve prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: The company allows all Dutch ships to trade to Surinam, upon paying two and a-half per cent. upon the value of their cargo for a license; and only reserves to itself exclusively, the direct trade from Africa to America...This relaxation in the exclusive privileges of the company, is probably the principal cause of that degree of prosperity which that colony at present enjoys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that opening markets (licenses, free ports) or relaxing monopolies increases trade, raises prices for colonial produce, and fosters prosperity—examples: Surinam's license system; Curacoa and Eustatia as free ports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance from mother country mitigates oppressive control
rubrics_metrics.description: Their great distance from Europe has in all of them alleviated more or less the effects of this dependency...The situation has placed them less in the view, and less in the power of their mother country...Even the violent and arbitrary government of Spain has...been obliged to recall or soften the orders which had been given for the government of her colonies, for fear of a general insurrection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distance reduces effective oversight and enforcement by the mother state, allowing colonies greater de facto freedom to manage affairs, sometimes improving prospects by lessening oppressive interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecclesiastical burdens and mendicant friars impede prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: Their ecclesiastical government is extremely oppressive. Tithes take place in all of them, and are levied with the utmost rigour in those of Spain and Portugal. All of them, besides, are oppressed with a numerous race of mendicant friars, whose beggary...is a most grievous tax upon the poor people...Over and above all this, the clergy are, in all of them, the greatest engrossers of land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that heavy ecclesiastical taxation (tithes), religiously sanctioned mendicancy, and the clergy's landholding reduce poor people's resources, concentrate land, and hinder productive improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremonial expense of government fosters vanity and permanent taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: The sums spent upon the reception of a new viceroy of Peru, for example, have frequently been enormous. Such ceremonials are not only real taxes paid by the rich colonists upon those particular occasions, but they serve to introduce among them the habit of vanity and expense upon all other occasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that extravagant civil ceremonials act as impromptu taxes and create social norms of luxury that generate ongoing private taxes (expenditure) and private luxury, undermining accumulation and economic discipline.
